title: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026
official_title: An Act to impose sanctions and other measures with respect to the Russian Federation, as championed by the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham, and for other purposes.
summary: The Senate replaced this bill, which the House passed as an early-childhood educator tax deduction, with the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. It directs the President to sanction Russian government officials, military leaders, state banks, and energy companies, block their U.S. assets, impose tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on countries that keep buying Russian oil or gas, and extend the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 to 2031.
brief: Directs the President to sanction Russia's officials, banks, and energy sector and to impose tariffs up to 500% on Russian goods, and extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 to 2031.

top_lines.headline: Russia Sanctions Regime
subs: Blocks assets and revokes U.S. visas for Russian officials and military chiefs
Sanctions the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank
Targets shadow-fleet tankers moving Russian oil and their insurers

top_lines.headline: Tariffs and Energy Bans
subs: Up to 500% duty on all goods imported from Russia
Up to 100% duty on countries buying Russian oil or gas
Bans Russian uranium imports and new U.S. energy investment in Russia

top_lines.headline: Iran Extension, Waivers, and Sunset
subs: Extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 from 2026 to 2031
Russia sanctions expire 5 years after enactment
President may waive or lift sanctions, subject to a congressional veto

likelihoodReason: This started as a House bill from a Democratic sponsor with 23 cosponsors and was rewritten by the Senate into a Russia-and-Iran sanctions substitute, which now needs the House to concur in the Senate's text. The up-to-500% tariffs on Russian goods and the secondary up-to-100% tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil or gas are the provisions most likely to draw opposition from trade-focused members, and are the main friction to final passage.

sections.label: Title I — Sanctions with respect to the Russian Federation

items.main: Requires the President to block the U.S. assets of, and deny entry to, Russian officials, military commanders, and oligarchs within 30 days.
items.detail: Section 102 lists officials from the president and defense minister to intelligence directors and military-district commanders, plus oligarchs and foreign persons aiding Russia's defense industrial base. It orders blocking of their property under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and makes them inadmissible to the U.S. with visas revoked. The President must repeat the review every 180 days.

items.main: Imposes sanctions on the Central Bank of Russia and state banks such as Sberbank and Gazprombank, and on foreign banks that deal with them.
items.detail: Section 103 requires blocking property and correspondent-account restrictions on the named Russian state banks within 30 days and bars U.S. persons from transacting with them. Foreign financial institutions that engage in significant transactions with those banks also face sanctions, unless the Treasury Secretary finds it inconsistent with U.S. economic or foreign-policy interests.

items.main: Sets tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on countries that keep buying Russian oil or gas.
items.detail: Section 112 raises duties on all goods imported from Russia, including oil, gas, and coal, to up to 500% ad valorem. Section 113 lets the President tariff up to 100% the goods of the 5 largest importers of Russian crude or gas, or countries facilitating Russian oil-sanctions evasion, with a carve-out for a country whose imports of Russian gas were under 15% of Russia's total annual gas exports and that has taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Sections 107 through 111 also ban new U.S. investment, energy exports, sovereign-debt purchases, and Russian uranium imports.

items.main: Extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 by changing its expiration from 2026 to 2031.
items.detail: Section 201 amends Section 13(b) of the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 by striking 2026 and inserting 2031. This is the bill's only Iran-related provision, and Section 203 exempts it from the five-year sunset applied to the rest of the division.

items.main: Lets the President waive or terminate the sanctions subject to a congressional joint resolution of disapproval, and sunsets the Russia sanctions after five years.
items.detail: Section 115 allows a waiver on a written national-interest certification to Congress. Section 117 lets the President terminate sanctions after certifying, for Russia, a peace agreement accepted by the Government of Ukraine and an end to hostilities, subject to a 30-day congressional review and a possible joint resolution of disapproval. Section 203 terminates the sanctions division, except the Iran extension, five years after enactment.

underreported.section: Section 201 — Extension of the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996
underreported.summary: Extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 from 2026 to 2031, inside a bill whose title and Title I otherwise address only Russia.
underreported.why_unreported: The Act is named for sanctioning Russia and Iran, but Iran appears only in this single date-change provision placed under Title II, 'Other matters.'

underreported.section: Section 114(k) — Exception for activities of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration
underreported.summary: Exempts NASA activities, and the supply of Russian products or services for NASA and other non-Defense space launches, from every sanction in Title I.
underreported.why_unreported: A blanket Russia-sanctions title preserves continued U.S.-Russia space-launch cooperation, an effect not apparent from the title's stated purpose.

underreported.section: Section 103(e) — Treatment of immobilized Russian sovereign assets
underreported.summary: States that U.S. and foreign banks holding immobilized Russian sovereign assets need not return interest earned that is due to Russia, and exempts loans to Ukraine serviced with those assets' proceeds.
underreported.why_unreported: Written as a rule of construction inside the bank-sanctions section, it governs the disposition of frozen Russian central-bank assets and financing for Ukraine, distinct from imposing new sanctions.

underreported.section: Division B — Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions
underreported.summary: The bill keeps a division headed for the original early-childhood educators' deduction; the Senate struck only section 1 and inserted the sanctions division as Division A.
underreported.why_unreported: The measure retains the House-passed educator-deduction subject as Division B while its operative new content, Division A, is the Russia and Iran sanctions regime.

gaps: Section 113 orders tariffs on the 5 largest importers of Russian oil and gas but names none of those countries in the text.
The bill requires most sanctions within 30 days of enactment but appropriates no funds for implementation.
The title covers Iran, but the bill's only Iran measure is changing the Iran Sanctions Act's date, addressing no new Iran conduct.
Section 103 lets the Treasury exempt foreign banks from sanctions when it is not in U.S. interests but states no criteria for that determination.

added: A sanctions regime targeting Russian officials, military, oligarchs, banks, and energy, enforced through property blocking and visa bans
Tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian oil or gas
Bans on new U.S. investment in Russia, U.S. energy exports to Russia, purchases of Russian sovereign debt, and Russian uranium imports
modified: Iran Sanctions Act of 1996: expiration date changed from 2026 to 2031
H.R. 5334's official title changed to an Act imposing sanctions on the Russian Federation, named for the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham
